title: Not this, not this
hookLine: the Upanishad describes the ultimate only by saying what it is not

cards: Try describing a silence. You can't say what it sounds like, because it doesn't sound like anything. All you can do is list what's missing: no traffic, no voices, no engine idling down the street.
Take enough away, and the other person knows exactly what you mean. One of the Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka, tries this with the biggest subject of all.
It reaches for the ultimate reality, and its answer is two words, said twice.

teach.b: Before it gets to the two words, the passage pictures the form of the person within, in a run of vivid images: like a saffron-colored cloth, like white wool, like a flame, like a white lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning.
Bright, beautiful, quick. Each one catches a glimpse. Second, the turn.
Then the text stops and says, in effect: now the teaching.
Not this, not this. In Sanskrit, neti neti, a phrase read as two small words run together, na and iti: not thus. All those images were pointing.
None of them is the thing. Third, why that isn't a shrug. You might hear not this, not this as giving up.
The text hears it the other way: there is nothing higher than this not-this. The refusal is the teaching.
Whatever you can picture, point at or put in a sentence is smaller than what the passage is after, so the honest description keeps saying no to every description. Fourth, where it leads.
The same passage gives a name for what can't be named: the truth of truth.
And some Hindu schools, especially Advaita Vedanta, use neti neti as a practice of the mind. Set aside the body: not this. Set aside the thoughts: not this.
Set aside the feelings: not this. What remains when you've said no to everything you can observe, they say, is the one doing the observing. The method is subtraction, all the way down.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers use neti neti as a method of inquiry, setting aside the body, thoughts and feelings as 'not this' to point toward the self that observes them.

o: not this, not this: saying no to every description
a mantra repeated to fall asleep peacefully
a chant for clearing away bad luck from a home

games.q: inside the passage — tap the pairs.
p: a name for what can't be named
uses neti neti as a practice

s: neti neti is a way of giving up on the question
the text says there is nothing higher than this not-this: the refusal is the teaching.
the passage offers vivid images before it says not this
a saffron cloth, white wool, a flame, a lotus, a flash of lightning.
the passage gives no name at all for what it points to
after not this, not this, it gives one: the truth of truth.

games.q: the passage has just pictured the person within as lightning, a flame and a lotus. what does it do next?
o: says the lightning was the right one.
games.why: it turns: now the teaching, not this, not this. none of the pictures is the thing.

practice: Let the breath find its own pace, and as each thing arrives, a sound, a thought, a plan, an itch, notice it and say inwardly: not this.
You're not pushing anything away, only declining to call it the whole story; between the not-thises, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, the quiet can be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Neti neti. Sanskrit for not this, not this: the Upanishad's way of pointing at the ultimate by saying no to every description of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: not this, not this (na iti, not thus), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3.6.

carryVoice: Your line: the refusal is the teaching. Saffron, wool, flame, lotus, lightning, and then: not this. See you tomorrow.
